```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
source("../R/ch01-figures.R")   # for the dual-axis callback (fig_spurious_ie)
source("../R/ch02-figures.R")
options(scipen = 999, width = 90, pillar.print_min = 6)

music_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wu-rds/MA2026/main/data/music_data_fin.csv"
music_raw <- read_csv2(music_url)
music_data <- music_raw |>
  mutate(
    genre    = as.factor(genre),
    label    = as.factor(label),
    explicit = factor(explicit, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("not explicit", "explicit")),
    top10    = factor(top10, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("no", "yes")),
    artist_id = as.character(artist_id),
    expert_rating = factor(expert_rating,
                           levels = c("poor", "fair", "good", "excellent", "masterpiece"),
                           ordered = TRUE),
    release_year = as.integer(format(release_date, "%Y"))
  ) |>
  rename(artist = artistName, track = trackName)
```

# 2.1 A first conversation with your data {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## Your first day in the data team {.midsize}

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
The head of A&R at a record label hands you a data set of tracks from the streaming charts:

> *"What is going on in the charts?"*

-   Which genres dominate?
-   How concentrated is success?
-   What distinguishes the hits from the rest?
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: keybox
**Driving question of this chapter:** *What is going on?* — the **descriptive** question from §1.3.

Before any model: **look at the data**. Description is where the problems are caught.
:::
:::
:::

## Four data sets — one set of statistics {.midsize}

```{r anscombe-table}
knitr::kable(anscombe_table())
```

. . .

::: discussion
Same means, same standard deviations, same correlation. **Are these four data sets alike?**
:::

## Summaries compress — pictures reveal {.midsize}

```{r anscombe-fig, fig.width=12.8, fig.height=3.8}
fig_anscombe()
```

::: keybox
A noisy line, a perfect curve, a line with one outlier, a "relationship" created by a single point — **identical summary statistics**. Good description always uses **both** numbers and pictures.
:::

::: source
Anscombe (1973), *The American Statistician* — built-in R data set `anscombe`.
:::

## The data: tracks in the streaming charts {.smaller}

**~67,000 tracks** that appeared in the Spotify charts, with 31 variables:

| Group | Variables |
|---|---|
| Identifiers | `isrc`, `artist_id`, `artistName`, `trackName` |
| Chart performance | `streams`, `weeks_in_charts`, `n_regions`, `top10` |
| Audio characteristics (0–100) | `danceability`, `energy`, `speechiness`, `instrumentalness`, `liveness`, `valence` |
| Track properties | `tempo`, `song_length`, `song_age`, `explicit`, `release_date`, `genre`, `label` |
| Other platforms & reach | `youtube_views`, `tiktok_counts`, `shazam_counts`, `n_playlists`, artist-level followers & listeners |
| Expert judgment | `expert_rating` (poor – fair – good – excellent – masterpiece) |

::: notes
Continuity: this is the Spotify world from §1.7. Don't read the table — point at the groups; the details come up as we use them.
:::

# 2.2 Getting data into R {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## Reading the data {.midsize}

```{r read-demo, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

music_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wu-rds/MA2026/main/data/music_data_fin.csv"
music_data <- read_csv2(music_url)
```

. . .

::: discussion
Why `read_csv2()` and not `read_csv()`? **What do you expect to happen** with `read_csv()`?
:::

::: notes
Let them guess, then run the next slide live. The European convention: comma = decimal mark, so columns are separated by semicolons.
:::

## An import can fail silently {.midsize}

```{r wrong-import, echo=TRUE}
wrong_import <- read_csv(music_url)
dim(wrong_import)
```

. . .

| Convention | Columns separated by | Decimal mark | Function |
|---|:-:|:-:|---|
| International | `,` | `.` | `read_csv()` |
| European | `;` | `,` | `read_csv2()` |

::: keybox
**No error ≠ correct.** Worse variants go unnoticed: `3,14` silently becoming `314`. Always **inspect right after importing**.
:::

## A first look {.smaller}

```{r glimpse-demo, echo=TRUE}
music_raw |>
  select(streams, danceability, genre, label, release_date, expert_rating) |>
  glimpse()
```

. . .

```{r summary-demo, echo=TRUE}
summary(select(music_raw, streams, song_length))
```

::: notes
glimpse() is THE function after an import: plausible number of columns? numbers as <dbl>, text as <chr>, dates as <date>? Then point at streams in summary(): mean more than 20x the median — "hold that thought until 2.6".
:::

## Other formats — same logic {.smaller}

| Format | Package | Function |
|---|---|---|
| CSV (international / European) | readr | `read_csv()` / `read_csv2()` |
| Other delimiters | readr | `read_delim("file.txt", delim = "\t")` |
| Excel | readxl | `read_excel("file.xlsx", sheet = "Sheet1")` |
| SPSS / Stata | haven | `read_sav()` / `read_dta()` |
| Qualtrics export | qualtRics | `read_survey()` → group project |
| Web pages / APIs | rvest / jsonlite | see the course book *(optional)* |

::: keybox
Files in your project folder are read by their **relative path**: `read_excel("data/survey.xlsx")` — no `setwd()` needed inside an RStudio Project.
:::

## What is a row? {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Tidy data** (Wickham, 2014):

1.  Each **variable** is a column
2.  Each **observation** is a row
3.  Each **value** is a cell
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: keybox
Before any analysis, answer explicitly: **what does one row represent?** — the **unit of observation** (cf. "unit of analysis" in §1.8). Here: one row = one track. *Does that really hold?* → §2.5
:::
:::
:::

```{r tidy-example}
untidy <- tibble(
  track = c("Track A", "Track B"),
  Jan = c(120, 80), Feb = c(135, 70), Mar = c(150, 65)
)
tidy <- untidy |>
  pivot_longer(cols = Jan:Mar, names_to = "month", values_to = "streams")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Untidy:** one column per month — "month" is hidden in the column names

```{r tidy-untidy-table}
knitr::kable(untidy)
```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
**Tidy:** one row per track and month

```{r tidy-tidy-table}
knitr::kable(tidy)
```
:::
:::
:::

# 2.3 Variables and levels of measurement {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## Levels of measurement: categorical {.smaller}

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 16% 42% 42%; gap: 0.6em; align-items: center;"}
::: {style="background: #0f5da8; color: white; font-weight: 700; text-align: center; padding: 1.2em 0.3em; border-radius: 6px;"}
Nominal
:::

::: {style="border: 2px solid #0f5da8; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.4em 0.8em;"}
-   Numbers only serve as **labels** for identification and categorization
-   They do not reflect the **amount** of a characteristic
-   Two categories: **binary**
-   Permissible operation: **counting**
:::

::: {style="border: 2px solid #0f5da8; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.4em 0.8em; text-align: center;"}
E.g., **starting numbers** in a race

![](../img/boat_3.png){width="31%"} ![](../img/boat_2.png){width="31%"} ![](../img/boat_1.png){width="31%"}

7 · 11 · 3
:::

::: {style="background: #0f5da8; color: white; font-weight: 700; text-align: center; padding: 1.2em 0.3em; border-radius: 6px;"}
Ordinal
:::

::: {style="border: 2px solid #0f5da8; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.4em 0.8em;"}
-   Numbers indicate the **relative position** (order)
-   …but not the **size of the differences**
-   Also: **greater / less than**; percentile-based statistics such as **median** and **quartiles**
:::

::: {style="border: 2px solid #0f5da8; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.4em 0.8em; text-align: center;"}
E.g., **finishing order** in the race

![](../img/boat_1.png){width="31%"} ![](../img/boat_2.png){width="31%"} ![](../img/boat_3.png){width="31%"}

1st · 2nd · 3rd place
:::
:::

## Levels of measurement: continuous (metric) {.smaller}

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 16% 42% 42%; gap: 0.6em; align-items: center;"}
::: {style="background: #0f5da8; color: white; font-weight: 700; text-align: center; padding: 1.2em 0.3em; border-radius: 6px;"}
Interval
:::

::: {style="border: 2px solid #0f5da8; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.4em 0.8em;"}
-   **Differences** can be compared (equal intervals)
-   …but the **zero point is arbitrary**
-   Ratios are **not** meaningful
-   Also: **range, mean, standard deviation**
:::

::: {style="border: 2px solid #0f5da8; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.4em 0.8em; text-align: center;"}
E.g., **finishing clock time** (start: 14:00)

![](../img/boat_1.png){width="31%"} ![](../img/boat_2.png){width="31%"} ![](../img/boat_3.png){width="31%"}

14:07:06 · 14:14:12 · 14:15:12
:::

::: {style="background: #0f5da8; color: white; font-weight: 700; text-align: center; padding: 1.2em 0.3em; border-radius: 6px;"}
Ratio
:::

::: {style="border: 2px solid #0f5da8; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.4em 0.8em;"}
-   All properties of the scales above
-   **Absolute zero point**
-   Ratios are meaningful ("**twice as fast**")
-   All statistical techniques apply
:::

::: {style="border: 2px solid #0f5da8; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.4em 0.8em; text-align: center;"}
E.g., **time to finish** (minutes)

![](../img/boat_1.png){width="31%"} ![](../img/boat_2.png){width="31%"} ![](../img/boat_3.png){width="31%"}

7.1 · 14.2 · 15.2
:::
:::

::: notes
The punchline: SAME three boats, four different numbers — the level of measurement is a property of the measurement, not of the object. Clock times and times to finish carry the same information; the only difference is the zero point. Ask: did boat B finish "twice as late" as boat A? The question makes no sense for 14:14 vs. 14:07 — midnight is an arbitrary zero. Subtract the start time and it does: 14.2 minutes is twice 7.1 minutes. Setting a natural zero turns an interval scale into a ratio scale. And the median of the finishing order is 2nd place; its mean is meaningless.
:::

## Not every number is a quantity {.smaller}

| Level | Values express | Music data | Meaningful | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Nominal** | Categories, no order | `genre`, `label`, `artist_id` | = / ≠ | Frequencies, mode |
| **Ordinal** | Ordered categories | `expert_rating` | + < / > | + median, quantiles |
| **Interval** | Equal distances, arbitrary zero | release *year*, °C | + differences | + mean, SD |
| **Ratio** | Equal distances, natural zero | `streams`, `song_length` | + ratios | + coefficient of variation |

. . .

::: keybox
Nominal + ordinal = **categorical**; interval + ratio = **continuous**. The level decides which **summaries**, **charts** — and later **tests** — are meaningful. The mean `artist_id` is as meaningless as the mean phone number.
:::

## Your turn: classify these (2 min) {.midsize}

::: discussion
Nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio?

(a) Customer ID · (b) Satisfaction: "very dissatisfied" … "very satisfied" · (c) Price in € · (d) Payment method · (e) Year of first purchase · (f) Purchased (yes / no)
:::

::: notes
(a) nominal — despite being a number; (b) ordinal — rating scales with many points are often treated as interval in practice, but strictly ordinal; (c) ratio; (d) nominal; (e) interval (year zero is arbitrary); (f) nominal/binary — useful property: mean of a 0/1 variable = share of 1s.
:::

## Telling R the level of measurement {.smaller}

```{r types-demo, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
music_data <- music_raw |>
  mutate(
    genre    = as.factor(genre),                                     # nominal
    explicit = factor(explicit, levels = c(0, 1),
                      labels = c("not explicit", "explicit")),        # nominal (binary)
    artist_id = as.character(artist_id),                             # an ID is not a number
    expert_rating = factor(expert_rating,
                           levels = c("poor", "fair", "good", "excellent", "masterpiece"),
                           ordered = TRUE)                           # ordinal
  )
```

```{r types-out, echo=TRUE}
table(music_data$expert_rating)
```

::: keybox
As text, R would sort the ratings **alphabetically**; as an **ordered factor**, R knows that *good* lies between *fair* and *excellent*.
:::

# 2.4 Data handling {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## The verbs of data handling {.smaller}

| Verb | Does | Example question |
|---|---|---|
| `filter()` | keeps **rows** meeting a condition | Pop tracks with > 10M streams? |
| `select()` | keeps **columns** | only artist, title, streams |
| `arrange()` | **sorts** rows | the most-streamed tracks? |
| `mutate()` | creates / changes **columns** | streams in millions? release year? |
| `group_by()` + `summarise()` | condenses to **one row per group** | median streams per label? |
| `count()` | counts rows per group | tracks per genre? |
| `left_join()` | **combines** tables via a key | add label information |

::: keybox
Same logic everywhere: data frame in → **column names without quotes** → data frame out. Chained with the pipe `|>`: *"and then"*.
:::

## Chaining steps with the pipe {.midsize}

```{r pipe-demo, echo=TRUE}
music_data |>                                  # take the music data, then
  filter(genre == "Pop") |>                    # keep the pop tracks, then
  arrange(desc(streams)) |>                    # sort by streams, then
  select(artist, track, streams) |>            # keep three columns, then
  head(4)                                      # show the first four rows
```

::: notes
Live: change "Pop" to "Rock"; add a second condition streams > 1e8; replace desc(). Note `==` (double!) and that `%>%` from older tutorials/AI output does the same.
:::

## "… per …": group_by() + summarise() {.midsize}

```{r group-demo, echo=TRUE}
music_data |>
  group_by(label) |>
  summarise(
    n_tracks       = n(),
    median_streams = median(streams),
    share_top10 = scales::percent(mean(top10 == "yes"), accuracy = 0.1)
  )
```

::: keybox
The workhorse of descriptive analysis: **every question of the form "… per …"** has this shape.
:::

## Combining tables: left_join() {.midsize}

```{r join-demo, echo=TRUE}
label_info <- tibble(
  label      = c("Universal Music", "Sony Music", "Warner Music", "Independent"),
  label_type = c("Major", "Major", "Major", "Independent")
)
music_data <- music_data |> left_join(label_info, by = "label")
music_data |> count(label_type)
```

::: keybox
Keeps **all rows of the left table**; no match → `NA`. **Check the row count after every join** — a non-unique key duplicates rows silently.
:::

## Your turn (live coding, 8 min) {.midsize}

::: discussion
Using the verbs, answer:

1.  How many **hip-hop** tracks reached the **top 10**?
2.  Which **label** has the highest **median streams** among hip-hop tracks?
3.  Create a variable `streams_mio` (streams in millions) and show the five **rock** tracks with the most streams.
:::

::: notes
Circulate. Solutions: (1) music_data |> filter(genre == "HipHop/Rap", top10 == "yes") |> nrow(); (2) filter(genre == "HipHop/Rap") |> group_by(label) |> summarise(med = median(streams)) |> arrange(desc(med)); (3) mutate + filter + arrange + select + head(5). Encourage AI use for syntax — then ask one student to explain their pipe line by line.
:::

# 2.5 Not trusting your data too early {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## Five checks before you trust a data set {.midsize}

::: incremental
1.  **Did the import work?** Rows, columns, types — §2.2
2.  **Missing values** — including zeros that mean "unknown"
3.  **Impossible values** — ranges, dates, units
4.  **Duplicates** — is the identifier really unique?
5.  **Extreme values** — errors or information?
:::

. . .

::: keybox
…and one question beyond the checks: **how did the data come to be?**
:::

## Check 2: zeros that mean "unknown" {.midsize}

```{r na-demo, echo=TRUE}
sum(is.na(music_data))                              # missing values: none at all?
mean(music_data$youtube_views == 0)                 # share of tracks with 0 YouTube views
```

. . .

::: keybox
58% of charting tracks with **zero** YouTube views? Almost certainly **"no data"**, not "no views". **Disguised missing values** (revenue 0 for never-contacted customers, age 0 in the CRM) drag every average down. Recode: `na_if(youtube_views, 0)` — and report how many are missing.
:::

## Check 3: impossible values {.midsize}

```{r range-demo, echo=TRUE}
music_data |>
  summarise(first_release = min(release_date), last_release = max(release_date),
            min_length = min(song_length), max_length = max(song_length),
            min_tempo = min(tempo))
```

. . .

::: keybox
Releases in **2029**, a **1-second** song, a tempo of **0 bpm**. Some values are clearly errors, others merely unusual (intros, medleys) — **inspect individually** before deciding.
:::

## Check 4: what is a row, really? {.midsize}

```{r dup-demo, echo=TRUE}
music_data |> summarise(n_rows = n(), n_distinct_isrc = n_distinct(isrc))
```

. . .

::: keybox
The ISRC should identify a recording uniquely — yet there are **`r format(nrow(music_data) - n_distinct(music_data$isrc), big.mark = ",")` more rows than ISRCs**, and the rows differ in streams and chart weeks. Versions? Periods? Errors? Without documentation we cannot tell — but "one row = one recording" **does not hold**.
:::

## Check 5: outliers are not always errors {.midsize}

```{r top-demo, echo=TRUE}
music_data |> arrange(desc(streams)) |> select(artist, track, streams) |> head(4)
```

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: keybox
In markets for creative products, **a few hits account for a large share of consumption**. Here, the extremes are the story — check them, don't delete them.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: keybox
**Document, don't silently delete:** corrections in **code**, **explicit** flags instead of overwriting, **transparent** reporting of what changed.
:::
:::
:::

## How did the data come to be? {.midsize}

```{r selection-fig, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.3}
fig_selection_charts()
```

::: keybox
Only **charted** tracks are in the data. Catchiness and promotion are unrelated among all songs (left) — but **negatively related among the survivors** (right). Created purely by the selection.
:::

::: notes
Walk the logic: to make the charts, a song needs catchiness + promotion to be high; so a charting song with low promotion MUST be catchy, and vice versa. Callback: §1.5 mentioned "selection into the sample" as the second species of selection bias — here it is. Ask for more examples before revealing the next slide.
:::

## Survivorship is everywhere in marketing data {.midsize}

::: incremental
-   Successful **products** only (launch data of products still on the market)
-   **Customers who did not churn** (loyalty-program data)
-   **Companies that still exist** ("what do successful firms do?")
-   **Survey respondents** — who chooses to answer is itself a choice (→ your group project!)
:::

. . .

::: keybox
Add one question to every descriptive checklist: **who is *not* in my data — and why?** Relationships among the survivors can differ from those in the population you care about (*Berkson's paradox*).
:::

# 2.6 Summarizing data {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## Categorical variables: frequencies {.midsize}

```{r freq-demo, echo=TRUE}
music_data |>
  count(genre, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  head(5)
```

::: notes
Pop + hip-hop ≈ 77% of all tracks. Base R alternative: table() and prop.table() — in the book.
:::

## Conditional frequencies {.midsize}

```{r cond-demo, echo=TRUE}
music_data |>
  group_by(genre) |>
  summarise(n = n(), share_top10 = mean(top10 == "yes")) |>
  arrange(desc(share_top10)) |>
  mutate(share_top10 = scales::percent(share_top10, accuracy = 0.1))
```

::: keybox
Beware of **small groups**: a share computed from 80 tracks is far less reliable than one from 30,000 — made precise in Module 3.
:::

## Mean or median? {.midsize}

```{r center-demo, echo=TRUE}
music_data |>
  summarise(mean = mean(streams), median = median(streams),
            q25 = quantile(streams, 0.25), q75 = quantile(streams, 0.75))
```

. . .

::: discussion
"The average track has **7.3 million** streams." — Is this a good description of the typical track?
:::

. . .

::: keybox
No: a few mega-hits pull the mean up — the distribution is **right-skewed**. The **median** (~333,000) describes the typical track. Mean far above median → a few extremes dominate the average (sales, revenue, followers, streams).
:::

## Location, dispersion, shape — in one call {.smaller}

```{r describe-demo, echo=TRUE}
library(psych)
music_data |>
  select(streams, danceability, energy, valence, song_length) |>
  describe() |>
  select(n, mean, sd, median, min, max, skew)
```

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   **Location:** mean, median
-   **Dispersion:** SD, range, IQR, coefficient of variation (SD / mean)
-   **Shape:** skewness — `streams` ≈ 17: extremely right-skewed
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: keybox
**z-scores** express relative position: $z = (x - \bar{x}) / s$ → "1.5 SDs above the average track". Their link to probabilities: Module 3.
:::
:::
:::

# 2.7 Visualizing data {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## The grammar of graphics {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Every `ggplot2` chart is built from the same components, **layer by layer** with `+`:

1.  **Data** — `ggplot(music_data, …)`
2.  **Aesthetic mappings** — `aes(x = …, y = …, color = …)`
3.  **Geoms** — `geom_col()`, `geom_point()`, `geom_boxplot()`, …
4.  **Labels, scales, themes** — `labs()`, `scale_…()`, `theme_…()`
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r gg-min, echo=TRUE, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=2.6}
genre_shares <- music_data |>
  count(genre) |> mutate(share = n / sum(n))
ggplot(genre_shares, aes(x = genre, y = share)) +
  geom_col()
```
:::
:::

## From default to useful {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r gg-full, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
ggplot(genre_shares,
       aes(x = fct_reorder(genre, share), y = share)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0f5da8") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent,
                     limits = c(0, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of tracks",
       title = "Pop and hip-hop dominate the charts") +
  theme_minimal()
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r gg-full-out, fig.width=5.4, fig.height=4.2}
ggplot(genre_shares, aes(x = fct_reorder(genre, share), y = share)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0f5da8") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of tracks", title = "Pop and hip-hop dominate the charts") +
  theme_minimal()
```
:::
:::

::: keybox
Sorted bars · readable labels · percent axis · a title that **states the finding**, not the topic.
:::

## Which chart for which variables? {.smaller}

| To show … | Variables | Chart | geom |
|---|---|---|---|
| One distribution | categorical | Bar chart | `geom_bar()` / `geom_col()` |
| | continuous | Histogram, density, boxplot | `geom_histogram()`, `geom_density()`, `geom_boxplot()` |
| Groups compared | categorical × continuous | Boxplots, jittered points | `geom_boxplot()`, `geom_jitter()` |
| A relationship | continuous × continuous | Scatter plot | `geom_point()` |
| Two categoricals | categorical × categorical | Grouped / stacked bars of shares | `geom_col(position = "dodge")` |
| Change over time | time × continuous | Line chart | `geom_line()` |

::: keybox
A third variable: **color** (`aes(color = …)`) or **small multiples** (`facet_wrap(~ …)`).
:::

## Skewed data: the log scale {.midsize}

```{r hist-both, fig.width=12, fig.height=3.8}
lab_short <- scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())
p_raw <- ggplot(music_data, aes(x = streams)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#0f5da8") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = lab_short) +
  labs(title = "Linear axis", x = "Streams", y = "Number of tracks") + theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
p_log <- ggplot(music_data, aes(x = streams)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#0f5da8") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = lab_short) +
  labs(title = "Log scale", x = "Streams (log scale)", y = "Number of tracks") + theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
p_raw + p_log
```

::: keybox
On a log scale, each step **multiplies** (10K → 100K → 1M). Makes skewed distributions readable — **always label it** in the axis title.
:::

## Comparing groups: boxplots {.midsize}

```{r box-demo, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.4}
music_data |>
  mutate(genre = fct_lump_n(genre, n = 6, other_level = "Remaining genres")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(genre, streams, .fun = median), y = streams)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#dbe7f3", outlier.alpha = 0.15) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Streams (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15)
```

::: notes
Read one box: median line, box = middle 50% (IQR), whiskers to 1.5 IQR, dots beyond. Takeaway: medians differ by genre, but the spread WITHIN each genre dwarfs the differences BETWEEN them.
:::

## Charts are data-quality tools, too {.midsize}

```{r time-demo, fig.width=11, fig.height=3.6}
music_data |>
  count(release_year) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = release_year, y = n)) +
  geom_line(color = "#0f5da8", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#0f5da8", size = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Release year", y = "Number of tracks") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15)
```

::: discussion
Two things in this chart should make you suspicious. **Which?**
:::

::: notes
(1) The axis runs to 2029 — the impossible release dates. (2) The collapse in 2021 is not a drop in releases: the latest plausible release date is July 2021, the last year is incomplete. "Sales collapsed this month!" — the incomplete final period is a classic false alarm.
:::

## Honest visualization I: bars start at zero {.midsize}

```{r trunc-fig, fig.width=10.5, fig.height=4.2}
fig_truncated_axis()
```

::: keybox
Bars encode values by **length** — a truncated axis makes the lengths lie. (Points and lines encode by *position* and may start elsewhere — clearly labeled.)
:::

## Honest visualization II: dual axes {.midsize}

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r ie-callback, fig.width=6.8, fig.height=4}
fig_spurious_ie()
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
Remember this one from §1.4?

::: keybox
Two independently chosen y-axes let you make **almost any two series look related**. Alternatives: index both series (first year = 100), or two charts side by side.
:::

-   Also avoid: **3D effects**, **pies** with many slices, colors without meaning, unsorted categories, axes without units
:::
:::

# 2.8 From description to insight {.divider background-color="#0a3d6e"}

## "Do explicit tracks perform worse?" {.midsize}

```{r explicit-1, echo=TRUE}
music_data |>
  group_by(explicit) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_streams = median(streams))
```

. . .

::: discussion
Can we write *"explicit lyrics reduce streams"*? **What would you check first?**
:::

## Looking within genres {.smaller}

```{r explicit-2, echo=TRUE}
music_data |>
  mutate(genre = fct_lump_n(genre, n = 5, other_level = "Remaining genres")) |>
  group_by(genre) |>
  summarise(share_explicit      = mean(explicit == "explicit"),
            median_not_explicit = median(streams[explicit == "not explicit"]),
            median_explicit     = median(streams[explicit == "explicit"]))
```

::: keybox
The gap persists within each large genre — but its size **and the share of explicit tracks** vary strongly. Genre, label, artist popularity, and the selection into the charts are all candidate **confounders** (§1.5).
:::

## What we can — and cannot — write {.midsize}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Descriptive ✓**

*"Among the tracks in our chart data, those with explicit lyrics have a lower median number of streams than those without (about 94,000 vs. 385,000). The gap is visible within each large genre, but varies in size."*
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Causal ✗**

*"Explicit lyrics reduce streams."*

That would require comparing the **same** tracks with and without explicit lyrics — a counterfactual the data cannot provide (§1.2).
:::
:::

. . .

::: keybox
A good descriptive finding answers: **What** was measured? **How much** (numbers, not adjectives)? **Compared to what? For whom? With which caveat?** — and uses descriptive verbs: *is higher, differs, is associated with* — not *causes, drives, increases*.
:::

::: notes
AI note to say out loud: assistants write fluent descriptions and slide happily from "is associated with" to "drives". Check every sentence against the five questions and against your own output.
:::

## Learning check {.smaller}

1.  After `read_csv("file.csv")` on a file from a German Excel, the data frame has **one column**. Why — and what should you use instead?
2.  Mean revenue per customer: **€480**, median: **€95**. What does this tell you about the distribution? Which number describes the typical customer?
3.  A loyalty-program data set contains **only active customers**. Among them, those who received few discounts buy most often. Why might this pattern mislead?
4.  **True or false?** (a) A variable stored as a number can be nominal. (b) Outliers should always be removed. (c) The y-axis of a bar chart should start at zero. (d) A zero in a data set always means the quantity was zero.

::: notes
(1) European CSV: semicolons + decimal commas → read_csv2(). (2) Right-skewed; median. (3) Survivorship / selection into the sample: churned customers are missing — perhaps the loyal ones never needed discounts, while discount-receivers who churned are gone. (4) T, F, T, F.
:::
